routes.description: Establish that ethics requires objective moral value, categorical obligation, and trustworthy moral cognition, and that a good creator provides their necessary metaphysical and epistemic foundation better than secular humanism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if God can ground real human value and universally binding duties while explaining reliable access to moral facts, and if secular humanism supplies only contingent goals, instrumental rules, or natural causes of moral belief.

motionBridge.description: Show that the theistic account satisfies the requirements of an ethical foundation that secular humanism cannot satisfy, thereby making God the better foundation for ethics.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective moral properties and obligations require a nonphysical standard of goodness and an authority transcending individual people and societies.
Establish that genuine duties must bind agents who reject human well-being and cannot arise solely from chosen goals, self-interest, social participation, or instrumental facts.
Explain how creation by a good God can make fallible human moral faculties reliably responsive to real moral truths rather than merely adaptive or conditioned beliefs.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect intentional creation and image-bearing status to objective human worth, rights, responsibility, and reasons to restrain harmful conduct.
Show that the theistic foundation can guide or transform conduct and withstand objections drawn from disputed revelation, religious disagreement, or historical wrongdoing.

routes.description: Establish that secular humanism provides a public, evidence-responsive ethical framework grounded in human interests, relationships, and consequences, while the proposed God supplies neither a demonstrated moral ground nor a usable system.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if shared conditions and interests support fact-constrained moral judgment, correction, and cooperation without cosmic imperatives, and if adding God fails to derive coherent duties or improve practical ethical inquiry.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular humanism supplies the clearer and more workable foundation for ethics while the proposed divine alternative remains unsupported, indeterminate, or unnecessary.

centralBridges.description: Establish human well-being, autonomy, relationships, and shared social interests as an intelligible ethical standard without requiring intrinsic cosmic value.
Show that physical and social facts can objectively constrain which actions better advance human interests once moral inquiry concerns how humans affect one another.
Explain how evidence, empathy, reason, education, due process, and revision can identify errors and resolve disagreement without treating consensus as infallible.
Show that positing a generic God does not demonstrate moral facts, derive particular duties, solve amoral motivation, or provide stable access to agreed ethical rules.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how interdependence, reciprocal benefit, and enlightened self-interest can motivate concern and cooperation despite the absence of universal cosmic commands.
Account for how circular definitions, conflicting revelations, or expectations of divine authorization and forgiveness limit the alleged practical advantage of God-based ethics.

sections.title: Ethical foundation and objective moral reality
sections.rationale: This issue determines what an ethical foundation must explain and whether objective values and obligations require a transcendent divine ground or can be framed through human-centered standards.

sections.title: Categorical duty and goal-based obligation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether secular humanism can obligate agents who reject well-being, and whether social facts and involuntary participation can support duties beyond conditional means-end rules.

sections.title: Moral knowledge, evidence, and error correction
sections.rationale: This issue compares divine-design and naturalistic accounts of moral cognition, including how each foundation explains trustworthy judgment, fallibility, disagreement, and improvement.

sections.title: Human value, cooperation, and moral motivation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether human worth and reasons for restraint require intentional creation or can arise from relationships, empathy, interdependence, consequences, and reciprocal interests.

sections.title: Practical guidance and foundational coherence
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether either foundation yields usable and consistent guidance in hard cases, including hidden wrongdoing, violence, disputed revelation, historical failures, and institutional intervention.
